e.t: This word describes someone or something that lacks steadiness—restless, unsettled, or unstable rather than firm and consistent. It can describe an unsettled condition that does not remain constant. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in James: once rendered “unstable” and once “restless.” The surrounding verse determines how that lack of steadiness is expressed, but the central idea remains absence of stability.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “revived,” “to become alive again,” or “to revive.” It describes life returning or something becoming active again after having been dead, lifeless, or inactive. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, appearing once in Luke and once in Romans. Depending on the sentence, it can describe a person becoming alive again or something that had been dormant coming to life. Its precise force in either verse is shaped by the surrounding passage.

This word means “folly”: foolishness or a lack of sound judgment. It is a noun that names an irrational or senseless way of thinking or acting. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Luke and 2 Timothy. The word itself identifies conduct or thinking as foolish, but the surrounding verse determines what particular foolishness is being described. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: folly is behavior or reasoning marked by poor judgment rather than wisdom or good sense.

e.t: This word means “to lead away”—to guide or take someone from one place or situation to another. It can describe ordinary direction, as when a path leads people toward a destination, or the removal and escort of a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times and is used for both being led along a way and being taken away under someone’s authority. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on who is leading, who is being led, and where the movement is directed.

This word means “removal,” referring to the taking away or putting aside of something. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in 1 Peter and once in 2 Peter. Its basic sense is therefore an act of removing rather than a person, place, or object. The precise force of the word in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the withdrawal, setting aside, or taking away of something.

e.t: To choke means to block or cut off breathing, preventing someone or something from continuing normally. In the Greek New Testament, this word expresses a forceful interruption rather than merely a difficulty or delay. It occurs twice, both in Luke, so its use is limited to those two passages. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular situation in each occurrence, but the central meaning remains consistent: to choke. This word means “enough” or “sufficient”: an amount or measure that meets what is required. It describes something as adequate rather than lacking, and it can mark a limit—what is enough for a situation or purpose. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing twice in Matthew and once in 1 Peter. Its exact force in any sentence is determined by the surrounding words, but its central idea remains that something has reached the needed measure.

e.t: This word means “to play the flute,” describing the action of producing music with a flute. It refers to flute playing rather than to a particular song, performance, or emotional response. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 11:17, Luke 7:32, and 1 Corinthians 14:7. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

e.h: A Word for Here or There
e.t: This word points to a place, meaning “here” or “there.” It functions as a location word, directing attention toward where someone or something is, or toward a place being discussed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Matthew, Luke, and Acts. Its exact force—whether indicating a nearby place or another location—depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central purpose is to identify place rather than describe a person, action, or quality.

me: Verb, second Aorist, Passive, iMperative, second, Singular

e.t: This word means “be reconciled” or “to become reconciled.” It expresses the movement from estrangement or conflict toward restored peace between people. In a sentence, it refers to reconciliation rather than leaving a damaged relationship unresolved. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 5:24. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific force intended there.

Righteousness refers to what is right and upright before God. In the New Testament, this word can describe righteousness itself, or something done or directed toward righteousness. It appears 92 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that it is an important term across the writings, especially in Romans. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains righteousness: right standing and right conduct as defined by God’s revealed will.

This word means “way out,” referring to an exit or means of escape from a difficult or confining situation. It presents deliverance as an available path through a circumstance, rather than simply the removal of the circumstance itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Corinthians 10:13 and Hebrews 13:7. Its exact force in either verse is clarified by the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a route leading out.

The word describes something implanted—placed into another thing so that it becomes established there. Its central idea is something introduced inwardly rather than merely laid alongside or attached on the surface. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs only once, in James 1:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but the word itself points to what has been planted or inwardly established.

Epaenetus is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Romans 16:5. The available wording preserves the name as “Epaenetus,” with “Epenetus” also representing it in English. Because this is a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of the person named, not a broader concept that can be defined like an ordinary noun or verb.

This word describes what is last in order or lowest in rank, and it can refer to the final position in a sequence. Its meanings include “last,” “last/least,” and “least.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 52 times, covering both the idea of finality and the idea of being lowest or least among others. Its exact force depends on whether the sentence concerns order, time, or rank. The word appears from Matthew through Revelation, showing broad use across the New Testament.

This word means “ready.” It describes a person or thing in a condition of readiness for an expected action, event, or responsibility. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 17 times, showing a recurring emphasis on being ready rather than unprepared. The surrounding sentence determines what the person or thing is ready for, so its exact application varies by passage. Its central idea remains simple: readiness to respond when the appropriate time or need arrives.

This word refers to an argument, dispute, or controversy—an issue being debated rather than a calm exchange of information. It is used in the Greek New Testament for matters that can lead to disagreement and contentious discussion. The word occurs seven times across seven New Testament verses, including three occurrences in Acts and additional uses in John, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

me: Verb, Present, Passive, iMperative, second, Plural

e.t: This word means “to alarm” or “to be alarmed.” It describes the act of causing fear or distress, and it can also describe a person becoming troubled or frightened. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in passages addressing disturbing reports or claims that could unsettle believers. Its basic sense focuses on emotional agitation: someone is shaken inwardly rather than remaining calm. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on causing alarm or on experiencing it.

“Iconium” is the name of a city mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a place name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. The name occurs six times in the New Testament: five times in Acts and once in 2 Timothy. Its meaning is therefore geographic and specific—it identifies Iconium as a location in the accounts where it appears, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the details of what happened there.

The word means “little fish,” referring to small fish rather than fish in a broad, unspecified sense. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Matthew 15:34 and once in Mark 8:7. Its meaning is concrete and straightforward: it identifies small fish. The surrounding details of either passage must be read from the verse and its context, but the word itself carries this simple meaning.

This word means “slander”: speech that unfairly harms another person’s reputation. It describes false, damaging, or malicious talk directed against someone rather than honest correction or a careful report. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in 2 Corinthians and once in 1 Peter. Its basic meaning remains focused on harmful speech about others, while the surrounding verse determines the precise situation being addressed.

This word describes something as “better” or “greater” than another thing. It is a comparative expression, marking a higher quality, value, condition, or rank rather than merely describing something in general. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 19 times across 18 verses, with especially frequent use in Hebrews. Its precise force—whether better in quality or greater in standing—depends on what is being compared in the surrounding sentence.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: “To burst” means to break open suddenly, or to open with force. This Greek New Testament verb describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. Its related gloss, “to burst open,” makes clear that the word can emphasize the opening or rupture itself. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 1:18. The precise force in that verse belongs to its surrounding context, but the word’s basic idea is a sudden bursting open.

This word means grief or sorrow—the painful sadness a person feels in response to distress, loss, or troubling circumstances. It is a noun describing an inward experience of anguish rather than an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times, especially in passages that speak of deep emotional pain. Its meaning remains broad enough to describe personal sorrow as well as shared or heartfelt grief. The surrounding passage determines what caused the sorrow in each occurrence.

e.t: This word means “be sober” and “to be self-controlled”: to remain clear-minded, restrained, and spiritually alert rather than ruled by confusion or impulse. It describes a steady way of thinking and living that enables a person to respond faithfully and remain watchful. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including repeated instruction in 1 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, and 1 Peter. Its use as an instruction shows that sober self-control is an ongoing posture, not merely a temporary feeling or avoidance of drunkenness.

This word means “eighth,” identifying a person or thing as number eight in a sequence. It describes position or order rather than naming a separate object or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, consistently carrying this ordinal meaning. It appears in passages from Luke, Acts, 2 Peter, and Revelation, but its precise significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding verse and subject being counted.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “after” or “from behind,” describing something located behind another thing or following it in sequence. It can point to a position at the back, or to something that comes afterward. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, across seven verses, including passages in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Revelation. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on whether the surrounding sentence emphasizes location or order.

This word means “oath,” referring to a solemn promise or sworn pledge. It is a noun used when Scripture speaks of an oath as something spoken or made under a serious commitment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, from Matthew through James. Its basic meaning remains consistent across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation in which the oath is mentioned.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “when” or “when(-ever)”. It marks the time or circumstance in which something happens, connecting one part of a sentence with another. It may introduce a future situation, a repeated circumstance, or a point in time, so its exact force comes from the surrounding words. This is a frequently used word in the Greek New Testament, appearing 123 times. Its basic function remains simple: it tells the reader when an action, event, or condition occurs. Matthew 5:11 and Mark 12:25 are among its recorded occurrences.

This word means a fetter or foot shackle, an iron restraint used to bind a person’s feet or legs and restrict movement. It refers to a physical fastening rather than an inner attitude or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in two verses: twice in Mark 5:4 and once in Luke 8:29. Its precise force in either passage is understood from the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a device used to confine someone.

This word describes “wearing,” referring to the act or condition of having something worn. It is a noun-like expression focused on what is worn rather than on a person or object itself. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 1 Peter 3:3. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its discussion of outward adornment, but its basic meaning remains the act of wearing.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: “Bitterly” describes an action done with bitterness or in a bitter manner. It is an adverb, so it tells how something is done rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice, and both occurrences are rendered “bitterly.” Its basic sense points to the intense, painful, or sorrowful quality accompanying an action, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force in each occurrence. Pudens is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing a quality, action, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, and its English rendering is simply “Pudens.” The available lexical information gives no additional definition beyond this name. Its occurrence is in 2 Timothy 4:21, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain what is said about the person there.

Priscilla is a personal name referring to a woman named Priscilla. It functions as a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts 18: Acts 18:2, Acts 18:18, and Acts 18:26. The name is consistently rendered “Priscilla,” so its meaning is the identification of this particular person. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what she does or how she is presented in any one occurrence.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to bring out.” It describes the action of bringing something outward or making it come forth. In ordinary sentence use, it focuses on the movement from within or from one place into view, rather than merely possessing or holding something. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both within Luke 6:45, so its precise force there belongs to that passage’s surrounding wording. [p03:word:greek-nt:G4393:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G4393:occurrences]

“Reuben” is a personal name, referring to Reuben in the Greek New Testament. This word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Revelation 7:5. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself can be explained clearly, but its particular significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action.

This word means “chain”: a physical restraint or linked fastening used to hold someone or something. It presents the idea of binding rather than freedom, though the exact force of the word in a passage must be understood from its surrounding text. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:4. The word’s basic sense remains focused on a chain as a restraining object.

This word refers to Spain, a geographic region. It is a proper place-name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Romans 15, where Paul mentions Spain as part of his intended travel and ministry plans. The word itself identifies the destination; the surrounding passage is needed to understand Paul's fuller purpose in mentioning it.

e.t: This word means “to conform to” or “to conform to a pattern.” It describes the action of shaping one’s conduct or character according to a pattern or model. As a verb, it expresses an active process of taking a form that corresponds to something else. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 12:2 and 1 Peter 1:14. Its exact force in either passage is clarified by the surrounding verse and its wider context.

Tabitha is a personal name, referring to the woman named in Acts 9. This Greek New Testament word is not presented as a general description, action, or quality; it identifies one person. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts 9:36 and 9:40, and the English rendering preserves it as “Tabitha.” The name’s specific significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical function is simply to identify the person called Tabitha.

This word means “wall,” referring to a structure that separates, encloses, or forms a boundary. It is a noun naming a physical barrier rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 23:3. Its basic meaning is straightforward, while the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the speaker uses the image of a wall.

Hymenaeus is a personal name, referring to a man named in the New Testament. It does not describe a general quality, action, or object, but identifies a particular person. The name appears twice in the Greek New Testament: once in 1 Timothy and once in 2 Timothy. Because the verse text and surrounding passages are not included here, this cached meaning identifies the word’s basic function as a personal name rather than explaining everything said about the man in either passage.

e.t: This word means “be kind”: to act with kindness toward others. It describes a person’s gracious, considerate way of treating people, rather than merely expressing a feeling of goodwill. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 13:4, so its normal meaning is represented by this single occurrence. The word functions as an action, describing what someone does in relation to others. Its precise force in that verse is understood more fully from the surrounding passage.

This word means “to clear out” or “to scour”—to remove what is present so that something is thoroughly emptied or cleaned. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 3:17. As an action word, it describes decisive removal rather than a minor adjustment or partial cleaning. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is thorough clearing or cleansing.
